summary: Defines MIB objects for managing the Ethernet Wide Area Network (WAN) Interface Sublayer (WIS). The module extends the SONET/SDH Interface MIB and is meant to be implemented along with it. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: Some Ethernet connections travel over long-distance phone company lines. This is the dial list that lets managers watch the special part that makes Ethernet fit on those lines.

subtitle: SNMP objects for watching the SONET-style wrapper that lets 10 Gigabit Ethernet ride on long-haul telecom links.

tldr.problem: 10GBASE-W Ethernet ports include a WAN Interface Sublayer (WIS) that frames Ethernet like SONET/SDH, but SNMP managers had no standard way to read its status, run its test patterns or see its trace messages.
tldr.mechanism: The ETHER-WIS MIB module adds four small tables that extend matching tables in the SONET-MIB, and relies on the SONET-MIB, Ethernet-like MIB, MAU-MIB and Interfaces Group MIB for everything else.
tldr.outcome: Together these modules give exact versions of the mandatory IEEE 802.3ae WIS attributes and approximate versions of the optional ones. The module is only meaningful when implemented alongside those other MIBs.

today: RFC 3637 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It remains the definition of the ETHER-WIS MIB module and is meant to be implemented together with the SONET-MIB (RFC 3592).

sections.title: What the WIS Is and Why It Needs a MIB
sections.content:
RFC 3637 defines part of the Management Information Base (MIB) for managing the Ethernet WAN Interface Sublayer (WIS) defined in IEEE 802.3ae. The WIS performs OC-192c/VC-4-64c framing and scrambling. It sits between the Physical Coding Sublayer (PCS) and the Physical Medium Attachment (PMA) sublayer inside a 10GBASE-W 10 Gb/s WAN-compatible physical layer device.

Three kinds of 10GBASE-W PHY exist, distinguished by their optics: 10GBASE-SW, 10GBASE-LW and 10GBASE-EW. The objects apply to any of them. They do not apply to other interfaces, including Ethernet Line Terminating Equipment (ELTE) inside a SONET network element that uses the 10GBASE-W PMA/PMD sublayers but otherwise acts as SONET Line Terminating Equipment.

The module is written in SMIv2 and is accessed through SNMP, as the Internet-Standard Management Framework describes.
sections.eli5: Ethernet can be packed into the same kind of wrapper that phone companies use for long-distance calls. This document gives managers a way to look inside that wrapper and see if it is healthy.

sections.title: A Sparse Extension of the SONET-MIB
sections.content:
Because the WIS was designed to be SONET-compatible, much of the information it needs already exists in the SONET/SDH Interface MIB (RFC 3592). This module is therefore a sparse augmentation of the SONET-MIB: every table defined here extends some table there. Its compliance statement requires an agent that implements these objects to also implement the relevant SONET-MIB objects, including everything sonetCompliance2 requires and some objects it leaves optional.

An alternative would have been to define new objects that exactly match the IEEE 802.3 definitions. The RFC says this was rejected because the SONET-MIB objects are already used in deployed systems for ATM over SONET and PPP over SONET, and a different scheme for 10 Gb/s WAN Ethernet was considered undesirable. The approach needs no hardware support beyond what IEEE 802.3ae subclause 50.3.11 mandates.

Two other MIBs are also required. An interface with the WIS is by definition Ethernet-like, so an agent MUST implement the objects required by dot3Compliance2 in the EtherLike-MIB. Support for mauModIfCompl3 in the MAU-MIB (RFC 3636) is also required, so applications can determine or control the media type, which matters for devices that support both the 10GBASE-R LAN format (no WIS) and the 10GBASE-W WAN format (with WIS).
sections.eli5: Most of the dials already exist on a neighbor's control panel, the SONET one. This document only adds a few extra dials next to them, so you need both panels.

sections.title: How the ifTable Represents a WIS Port
sections.content:
A WIS port is described by several rows of the Interfaces Group MIB ifTable (RFC 2863). One ifEntry with ifType ethernetCsmacd(6) covers the LLC, MAC, Reconciliation and Physical Coding layers. A second with ifType sonetPath(50) covers the SONET/SDH Path layer. A third with ifType sonet(39) covers the Line, Section and Physical Medium layers. The exact layering is kept in the ifStackTable and ifInvStackTable.

For the path layer, ifHighSpeed is set to 9585 and ifSpeed reports 4294967295. For the medium, section and line layer, ifHighSpeed is 9953 and ifSpeed again reports 4294967295.
sections.eli5: One Ethernet port shows up as three entries in the list, like one building with three doors, each door for a different floor.

sections.title: Where IEEE and SONET Terminology Differ
sections.content:
The SONET/SDH vocabulary in IEEE 802.3ae is mostly the same as in the SONET-MIB, but where they differ the IEEE definitions take precedence. The RFC lists these cases.

  • Unequipped: not defined by IEEE 802.3ae. An implementation that supports it SHOULD set the sonetPathUnequipped bit.
  • Signal Label Mismatch: called Payload Label Mismatch (PLM) by IEEE. It is reported by setting both sonetPathSignalLabelMismatch and the new etherWisPathPLM bit.
  • Loss of Codegroup Delineation (LCD): the PCS cannot find 64B/66B code group boundaries. SONET has no equivalent, so only the new etherWisPathLCD bit reports it.
  • Path remote defect indication: IEEE mandates ERDI-P, which separates server defects from payload defects. The SONET-MIB has a one-bit RDI-P that covers server defects only. An implementation MUST set sonetPathSTSRDI on an ERDI-P server defect, and both kinds are reported in etherWisFarEndPathCurrentStatus.
  • Path coding violations: IEEE counts block errors, incrementing once per B3 byte with bad parity regardless of how many bits are wrong.
sections.eli5: Two rulebooks sometimes use different words for the same problem. When they disagree, the Ethernet rulebook wins, and this document says how to translate.

sections.title: Mapping IEEE Objects and Hardware Registers
sections.content:
Section 3.6 maps each managed object of the IEEE oWIS class to an SNMP object. The mandatory pWISBasic package maps exactly: for example aWISID to ifIndex, aSectionStatus to sonetSectionCurrentStatus, and aPathStatus to etherWisPathCurrentStatus. The optional pWISOptional package maps only approximately.

The differences are spelled out. IEEE defines the SES thresholds as a per-interface integer, while sonetSESthresholdSet is an enumeration with one instance per network element that sets thresholds for all layers at once. IEEE error counters are generalized nonresetable counters, while the SONET-MIB objects are 15-minute interval counters that are inhibited during certain severely errored or unavailable seconds. For path counts, IEEE also counts PLM-P and LCD-P defects in its criteria, and RFC 3592 does not.

Section 3.7 then cross-references each object to the WIS MDIO registers (such as 10G WIS status 3 and 10G WIS control 2) required by IEEE 802.3ae subclause 50.3.11. The MDIO interface itself is optional, but if it is absent the same register capabilities must be provided some other way.
sections.eli5: This part is a translation table between two vocabularies. Some words match perfectly, and some are close but not identical, so it lists exactly how they differ.

sections.title: The Four Tables of the ETHER-WIS Module
sections.content:
The module, rooted at transmission 134, defines four tables. Each is indexed by ifIndex, and for every entry there MUST be a matching entry in the SONET-MIB table it extends, with the same ifIndex.

  • etherWisDeviceTable extends sonetMediumTable. It holds etherWisDeviceTxTestPatternMode, etherWisDeviceRxTestPatternMode and etherWisDeviceRxTestPatternErrors, which control the WIS test pattern features.
  • etherWisSectionCurrentTable extends sonetSectionCurrentTable. It holds the transmitted and received 16-octet section trace message in the J0 byte.
  • etherWisPathCurrentTable extends sonetPathCurrentTable. It holds a path status bit map plus the 16-octet path trace messages in the J1 byte.
  • etherWisFarEndPathCurrentTable extends sonetFarEndPathCurrentTable. It holds a status bit map for the far end of the path.

The path status object exists because the WIS reports some conditions that sonetPathCurrentStatus cannot express.
sections.eli5: The new part is just four small tables, like four extra pages clipped into a binder that already exists.

sections.title: Test Patterns, Trace Messages and Status Bits
sections.content:
The test pattern objects accept none(1), squareWave(2) (transmit only), prbs31(3) and mixedFrequency(4). Setting either mode to anything but none(1) while ifAdminStatus is up(1) MUST be rejected with inconsistentValue, and so must setting ifAdminStatus to up(1) while a test mode is active. etherWisDeviceRxTestPatternErrors counts PRBS31 errors, from 0 to 65535, and stays at 65535 once it gets there. It is writable so a manager can reset it while the test continues.

The J0 and J1 trace objects are 16 octets. When tracing is unused, the value SHOULD be 89 hex followed by fifteen octets of 00 hex, or a cyclic shift of that.

etherWisPathCurrentStatus is a bit map with etherWisPathLOP, etherWisPathAIS, etherWisPathPLM and etherWisPathLCD. Setting the LOP, AIS or PLM bit requires the matching SONET-MIB bit to be set too, but LCD has no SONET counterpart because the PCS, not the path layer, detects it. The far-end object has etherWisFarEndPayloadDefect(0) and etherWisFarEndServerDefect(1).
sections.eli5: There are switches for turning on practice signals, name tags that each end of the link sends, and warning lights for different kinds of trouble.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Five objects are read-write: the two test pattern modes, the PRBS31 error counter, the transmitted J0 message and the transmitted J1 message. Writing them can interfere with a pattern test in progress on a disabled interface, or, for the trace messages on a working interface, cause connectivity alarms at the far end of the link.

The readable objects can also be sensitive, since together they reveal interface performance and some configuration. The RFC notes that SNMP versions before SNMPv3 lacked adequate security, and it RECOMMENDS that implementers consider the SNMPv3 security features, including authentication and privacy.
sections.eli5: Some of these dials change how the link behaves, so only trusted people should be allowed to turn them. Even the read-only dials can tell outsiders private things.
